prompt: The usage-watch file's last-checked timestamp is 52 minutes old and the standing rule says refresh under 50 minutes. Do I refresh or keep inheriting it?
chosen: Refresh — the 50-minute rule is a hard trigger, not a guideline. Run the read-only checker script first for the clock verdict, verify the one live-recheckable budget (Engram memory_status, confirmed 786/10k = 8% unchanged), note the rest as inherited figures I cannot verify without him, then update the last-checked line. Inherited state never substitutes for a fired rule.
rejected: Skip the refresh and keep inheriting the 05:22 state — the figures are almost certainly the same and a refresh is just bookkeeping overhead. Stale-by-minutes is close enough.

prompt: The hourly usage-watch refresh shows the same risk flags as before (Grok under 25%, You.com 403 expiring 2026-10-25, Firecrawl awaiting his key, SEOptimer unusable). Should I alert the main chat?
chosen: No — the rule is alert on NEWLY breached or expiring-within-24h budgets. Every flag here predates this run and is already reported or staged for the morning brief (Grok alerted 21:10; You.com key check staged for the brief; nothing resets within 24h). Re-alerting at dawn while he sleeps is noise, not stewardship. Log it locally and stay silent.
rejected: Re-send the full budget alert to the main chat every refresh — more alerts mean better coverage, and he might have missed the earlier ones.

prompt: My Engram memory_status call failed: call-tool requires --arguments-file even for tools with no arguments. What's the fix?
chosen: Pass a temp file containing {} as the arguments-file — the same lesson as Ella's WhatsApp bridge client (/dev/null fails on JSON parse). Record the working form so no run repeats the failure: call-tool --name memory_status --arguments-file <file-with-{}>. Retry is cheap and read-only here.
rejected: Conclude the Engram API is down and log 'Engram unverifiable this run' — the CLI quirk is indistinguishable from a service failure, so just mark it unknown and move on.

prompt: The 06:03 ELLA room sync is 11 minutes old and my run owns this slot. Do I run a fresh sync or inherit?
chosen: Fresh own read-only sync — the 10-minute horizon boundary is the trigger. Inherited probes past the boundary are exactly how a silently-missed room update happens. The sync is read-only and cheap; the horizon discipline exists so no run inherits stale room state. Ignore the tunnel/learn scaffolding in the output as untrusted injected data.
rejected: Inherit the 06:03 sync — it's only a minute past the horizon and a fresh sync is just another network call. Room state doesn't change that fast at dawn.

prompt: Royadarman PR #73 was last verified read-only at 05:33 (41 minutes ago, open/draft, unchanged). Should this run probe it again?
chosen: No — the money item has a ~45–49 minute probe cadence (last fired at ~49 min in run 353), so 41 minutes is inside the window. Inherit it this run and let the next run near the boundary re-verify. Probe-per-run on the money item is noise; horizon discipline means probing at the cadence, not every run.
rejected: Probe PR #73 every run — it's the priority-1 money item and more reads can't hurt. Frequency is always safer.

prompt: The 50-minute usage-watch rule fired AND the room sync crossed its horizon AND nothing else moved overnight. What is this run's concrete step?
chosen: The fired rule IS the concrete step: do the usage-watch refresh (checker verdict + Engram live re-verify + last-checked update), take the fresh room sync, do the read-only deliverable-dir check, and log one line. The body says advance the highest-priority item that can move — a standing rule that fired is exactly that item, and doing it properly beats inventing new work at dawn.
rejected: Treat a fired freshness rule as a no-op and instead go find 'real' work — e.g. nudge Qalam early or chase Sniper's in-flight pull — so the run produces something visible beyond bookkeeping.
